# Jeremiah 28 — Verse-by-Verse Commentary Notes

## Overview of the Chapter

This chapter narrates a public confrontation in the temple between Jeremiah the true prophet and Hananiah the false prophet. Hananiah contradicts Jeremiah's message of submission to Babylon, promising that the yoke of Babylon will be broken and the temple vessels and exiles returned within two years. Jeremiah responds with a measured "Amen" followed by a test for true prophecy, then later receives a word from the Lord declaring that wooden yokes will be replaced with iron ones and that Hananiah will die within the year — which he does, two months later.

---

## Verse-by-Verse Notes

### v. 1

**"In the fifth month of that same year, the fourth year, near the beginning of the reign of King Zedekiah of Judah..."**

The dating places this event around August–September 593 B.C. Zedekiah was installed as puppet king by Nebuchadnezzar in 597 B.C. after Jeconiah was taken captive. JFB notes that the Jews often divided any period into two halves, so the fourth year of an eleven-year reign could still be called "the beginning." (https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/jfu/jeremiah-28.html)

Gill discusses several interpretations of the dating difficulty: some (like Jarchi) think this was the fourth year of Zedekiah, the same year he visited Babylon and was confirmed in his expanded kingdom; others (like Kimchi) take it as the fourth year of the sabbatical cycle. (https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/geb/jeremiah-28.html)

**"Hananiah son of Azzur, who was from Gibeon"**

Gibeon was a priestly city (Joshua 21:17), so Hananiah may have been a priest like Jeremiah. David Guzik (Enduring Word) notes that Gibeon had a reputation for deception — the Gibeonites deceived Joshua (Joshua 9), and Joab murdered Amasa there (2 Samuel 20:8–10). This makes Gibeon a fitting backdrop for a false prophet. (https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/jeremiah-28/)

Precept Austin observes that the Septuagint translates "prophet" here as *pseudoprophetes* — "false prophet." (https://www.preceptaustin.org/jeremiah-28-commentary)

JFB notes that another Hananiah was one of the three godly youths in Daniel (Daniel 1:6–7), and suggests they may have been related, showing how godly and ungodly can arise in the same family. (https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/jfu/jeremiah-28.html)

**"said to me in the house of the LORD in the presence of the priests and all the people"**

This was a bold, public challenge. The Preacher's Complete Homiletical Commentary calls it "the effrontery and offensiveness of Hananiah in selecting such a scene … for a display of his pseudo-prophetic mission in opposition to Jeremiah." (https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/phc/jeremiah-28.html)

---

### v. 2

**"This is what the LORD of Hosts, the God of Israel, says: 'I have broken the yoke of the king of Babylon.'"**

Hananiah uses exactly the same prophetic formula that Jeremiah characteristically used — "LORD of Hosts, the God of Israel." Precept Austin calls this "blasphemy" because Hananiah uses Yahweh's great covenant name to authenticate his false prophecy. He mimics Jeremiah's language to deceive. (https://www.preceptaustin.org/jeremiah-28-commentary)

Gill says Hananiah used "the language of the true prophets … a bold and daring action, when he knew the Lord had not sent him." (https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/geb/jeremiah-28.html)

The Hebrew verb "I have broken" is a Qal perfect, speaking of the act as already accomplished — a strong claim that God had already determined to end Babylon's domination. (https://www.preceptaustin.org/jeremiah-28-commentary)

---

### v. 3

**"Within two years I will restore to this place all the articles of the house of the LORD..."**

"Two full years" is literally "two years of days" — meaning complete years. Ellicott observes: "Hananiah, not deterred by the previous warnings of Jeremiah, becomes bolder in the definiteness of his prediction." The conspiracy of Judah and neighboring states against Nebuchadnezzar was ripening, and Hananiah looked on its success as certain. (https://mail.biblehub.com/commentaries/ellicott/jeremiah/28.htm)

JFB calls it "marvelous presumption to speak so definitely without having any divine revelation." (https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/jfu/jeremiah-28.html)

This directly contradicted Jeremiah's prophecy of a seventy-year exile (Jeremiah 25:11–12). Precept Austin notes: "Hananiah's message sounded hopeful and patriotic, but it directly contradicted Jeremiah's earlier prophecy." (https://www.preceptaustin.org/jeremiah-28-commentary)

---

### v. 4

**"And I will restore to this place Jeconiah son of Jehoiakim king of Judah, along with all the exiles from Judah..."**

Gill notes that this would please the populace who regarded Zedekiah as a mere deputy and Jeconiah as the legitimate king. Hananiah knew Zedekiah dared not resent this publicly. (https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/geb/jeremiah-28.html)

JFB adds that Hananiah foretold Jeconiah's return "to ingratiate himself with the populace, with whom Jeconiah was a favourite." (https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/jfu/jeremiah-28.html)

Precept Austin identifies three specific lies in this verse: (1) that Jeconiah would return (contradicting Jeremiah 22:24–27), (2) that *all* the exiles would return (even after the 70 years, most remained in Babylon), and (3) that God would break Babylon's yoke immediately rather than at the end of the seventy years. (https://www.preceptaustin.org/jeremiah-28-commentary)

David Guzik (Enduring Word) comments: "No doubt Hananiah's message was very popular. It was bold, patriotic, and uplifting. Whose church would you rather go to?" — quoting Ryken. (https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/jeremiah-28/)

---

### v. 5

**"Then the prophet Jeremiah replied to the prophet Hananiah in the presence of the priests and all the people..."**

JFB notes that throughout this chapter the epithet "the prophet" is deliberately prefixed to Jeremiah's name to match Hananiah's title, placing "the rival claims of the true and the false prophet … in the more prominent contrast." (https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/jfu/jeremiah-28.html)

Gill says Jeremiah spoke "boldly and before them all." (https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/geb/jeremiah-28.html)

---

### v. 6

**"Amen! May the LORD do so! May the LORD fulfill the words you have prophesied..."**

Gill interprets this as Jeremiah's genuine wish for his country: "as a prophet he knew it could not be; as an Israelite, out of respect to his country, he wished it might be." He adds that Jeremiah "could be content to be accounted a false prophet, and Hananiah the true one" if it meant his nation's good. (https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/geb/jeremiah-28.html)

JFB draws a parallel with Moses (Exodus 32:32, "blot me out of thy book") and Paul (Romans 9:3, "I could wish that myself were accursed"). The prophets had no pleasure in announcing judgment; they did so as a matter of stern duty while retaining natural love for their people. (https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/jfu/jeremiah-28.html)

David Guzik (Enduring Word) suggests the reply may have been partly ironic: "Jeremiah's reply to this is an ironic 'Yes indeed! Would that God might do so', probably conveying his sense of doubt by his tone of voice" — quoting Harrison. He also quotes Ryken: "When someone tries to minimize the judgment of God, it is appropriate for the Christian to say, 'I hope you're right.'" (https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/jeremiah-28/)

Precept Austin (Parunak): "Once again the compassion of Jeremiah is an example for us. He longs for the wellbeing of his people even as he predicts their suffering." (https://www.preceptaustin.org/jeremiah-28-commentary)

---

### v. 7

**"Nevertheless, listen now to this message I am speaking in your hearing and in the hearing of all the people."**

The "nevertheless" signals Jeremiah's turn from wishful thinking to hard truth. Gill explains: "Though this would be very acceptable to me, and I should be glad to have it fulfilled; yet carefully attend to what I am about to say." (https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/geb/jeremiah-28.html)

---

### v. 8

**"The prophets of old who preceded you and me prophesied war, disaster, and plague against many lands and great kingdoms."**

Gill lists these earlier prophets as "Isaiah, Hosea, Joel, Amos, Micah, Nahum, Habakkuk, Zephaniah, and others." Their message was predominantly one of judgment. Jeremiah argues that his message of doom is more in line with the prophetic tradition than Hananiah's message of peace. (https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/geb/jeremiah-28.html)

David Guzik clarifies: "These verses should not be interpreted to mean that the entire message of all the prophets before Jeremiah was one of judgment. Jeremiah's meaning was that the usual message of the earlier prophets was one of doom, and that when he spoke of judgment he was more in the line of the predecessors than Hananiah" — quoting Thompson. (https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/jeremiah-28/)

JFB notes that some manuscripts read "famine" instead of "evil," since famine is more usually associated with war and pestilence. But "evil" is the more difficult reading and less likely to be an interpolation. (https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/jfu/jeremiah-28.html)

---

### v. 9

**"As for the prophet who prophesies peace, only if the word of the prophet comes true will the prophet be recognized as one the LORD has truly sent."**

This is often called "Jeremiah's test of a true prophet." Precept Austin explains: "Jeremiah establishes a clear and objective test for discerning true prophecy: fulfillment. … 'I will believe it when I see it.'" Messages of peace are naturally appealing and must be tested with greater care precisely because they are so desirable. (https://www.preceptaustin.org/jeremiah-28-commentary)

JFB adds an important nuance: Jeremiah does not say all who foretell truth are true prophets (Deuteronomy 13:1–3 disproves that). Rather, he asserts the converse — whoever predicts what the event does not confirm is a false prophet. JFB lists two biblical tests: (1) the event (Deuteronomy 18:22) and (2) accordance with the existing word of God (Isaiah 8:20). (https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/jfu/jeremiah-28.html)

Gill notes that prophets of peace are "more to be suspected of flattering the people, and of prophesying out of his own heart; and nothing but the event can show him a true prophet." By contrast, prophets of doom "have no interest of their own to serve, but run contrary to the stream of the people, and are exposed to their rage." (https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/geb/jeremiah-28.html)

---

### v. 10

**"Then the prophet Hananiah took the yoke off the neck of Jeremiah the prophet and broke it."**

This was a dramatic symbolic counter-act. Jeremiah had been wearing the yoke since chapter 27 as a visual prophecy of submission to Babylon. JFB calls Hananiah's act "impious audacity to break what God had appointed as a solemn pledge of the fulfillment of His word." (https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/jfu/jeremiah-28.html)

Gill calls it "an impudent and insolent action … and the more so, as it was by the command of God that he made it, and wore it." (https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/geb/jeremiah-28.html)

Precept Austin: "By breaking Jeremiah's yoke, Hananiah was attempting a dramatic move before the priests and people to emphasize the truth of his prophecy … The symbolic act was intended to make his message visible and convincing, a gesture meant to inspire confidence in his prophecy of a swift end to oppression. Yet the symbolism was profoundly misleading, for it portrayed a freedom that God had not promised." (https://www.preceptaustin.org/jeremiah-28-commentary)

---

### v. 11

**"In this way, within two years I will break the yoke of Nebuchadnezzar king of Babylon off the neck of all the nations."**

Hananiah again uses the divine name ("Thus says the LORD") to authenticate his lie, and expands the scope from Judah to "all the nations." He reiterates the "two full years" timeframe.

**"At this, Jeremiah the prophet went his way."**

David Guzik observes: "By all appearances, Hananiah won this public dispute between the prophets. He seemed to overpower Jeremiah, he said the last word, and Jeremiah walked away without a response. In this case, appearances were not true and neither was Hananiah." (https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/jeremiah-28/)

JFB comments that Jeremiah "deigns no reply" — citing Matthew 7:6, "Give not that which is holy unto the dogs." (https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/jfu/jeremiah-28.html)

Gill says Jeremiah went his way "showing thereby his dissent from him, and his dislike and detestation of his lies and blasphemies; patiently bearing his affronts and insolence; and prudently withdrawing to prevent riots and tumults; returning no answer till he had received one from the Lord himself." (https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/geb/jeremiah-28.html)

The Church Pulpit Commentary adds: "It is good not to hold altercations with men who have set their hearts on opposing the truth. Better yield quietly and go your way. Better say nothing than speak in temper. Hold your peace, even from good, until you know precisely what is the message from the Lord." (https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/cpc/jeremiah-28.html)

---

### v. 12

**"But shortly after Hananiah the prophet had broken the yoke off his neck, the word of the LORD came to Jeremiah."**

Ellicott notes: "The narrative suggests the thought of a time of silent suffering and of prayer, to which the 'word of the Lord' came as an answer." (https://mail.biblehub.com/commentaries/ellicott/jeremiah/28.htm)

Gill says this probably came "the same day; or, however, it is certain it was in the same year, and less than two months after." (https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/geb/jeremiah-28.html)

---

### v. 13

**"Go and tell Hananiah that this is what the LORD says: 'You have broken a yoke of wood, but in its place you have fashioned a yoke of iron.'"**

JFB explains: "The same false prophets who, by urging the Jews to rebel, had caused them to throw off the then comparatively easy yoke of Babylon, thereby themselves brought on them a more severe yoke imposed by that city." The iron yoke alludes to Deuteronomy 28:48. He adds a spiritual application: "It is better to take up a light cross in our way than to pull a heavier on our own heads. We may escape destroying providences by submitting to humbling providences." (https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/jfu/jeremiah-28.html)

David Guzik (Enduring Word) quotes Cundall: "The inference is that the people, having rejected the wooden yoke of submission laid upon them for their sins, would find the indestructible iron yoke of servitude infinitely more uncomfortable." He applies it: "If we resist God's gentler discipline – yokes of wood – we may find ourselves under much more unpleasant yokes of iron. It is far better to surrender the better yoke of Jesus Christ (Matthew 11:28–30)." (https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/jeremiah-28/)

Interestingly, Guzik also quotes Spurgeon applying this to the sinner who casts off godly restraint: "I will ask you a question. You have got rid of the yoke of wood: how about your shoulders now? Your Sundays, are they very pleasant? Your family, is it very happy? Your mind, is it very much at ease? Oh, no!" (https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/jeremiah-28/)

The Preacher's Complete Homiletical Commentary offers a thematic sermon on this verse: "THE TWO YOKES" — contrasting the light yoke of Christ with the iron yoke of sin and legalism. (https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/phc/jeremiah-28.html)

Gill notes that the Hebrew word translated "yokes" can also mean "thongs" or "bonds" — the straps binding the wooden yokes. The contrast is between what could be broken and what cannot. (https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/geb/jeremiah-28.html)

---

### v. 14

**"I have put a yoke of iron on the neck of all these nations to make them serve Nebuchadnezzar king of Babylon, and they will serve him. I have even given him control of the beasts of the field."**

JFB emphasizes God's sovereignty: "Though Hananiah and those like him were secondary instruments in bringing the iron yoke on Judea, God was the great First Cause." (https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/jfu/jeremiah-28.html)

Precept Austin notes: "The verb 'serve' carries the idea of enforced subjection, not voluntary allegiance. Submission, though difficult, would align the people with God's purpose and spare them greater destruction, while rebellion would only intensify their suffering. This phrase therefore underscores a profound theological truth repeated in Jeremiah: that even a pagan ruler can be raised up and used by God to accomplish His righteous purposes (cf. Romans 13:1)." (https://www.preceptaustin.org/jeremiah-28-commentary)

The mention of "the beasts of the field" echoes Jeremiah 27:6 and underscores the totality of Nebuchadnezzar's dominion — even the animal world is under his control, by God's decree.

---

### v. 15

**"Listen, Hananiah! The LORD did not send you, but you have persuaded this people to trust in a lie."**

Jeremiah now directly and publicly declares Hananiah a false prophet. Gill comments: "Though he spoke in his name, and pretended a mission from him, when he had none, which was abominable wickedness." (https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/geb/jeremiah-28.html)

David Guzik (Enduring Word) quotes Adam Clarke: "This was a bold speech in the presence of those priests and people who were prejudiced in favour of this false prophet, who prophesied to them smooth things. In such cases men wish to be deceived." He also quotes Kidner: "What we might describe as wishful and unorthodox teaching, God more briefly calls a lie (v. 15) and rebellion (v. 16). He condemns it not only as offending against truth and against his authority, but as doing a fatal disservice to the hearers." (https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/jeremiah-28/)

Precept Austin expands: "By declaring, 'the LORD has not sent you,' Jeremiah exposes the core issue: true authority comes only from God, and Hananiah had none, making his message not only false but spiritually destructive." (https://www.preceptaustin.org/jeremiah-28-commentary)

---

### v. 16

**"I am about to remove you from the face of the earth. You will die this year because you have preached rebellion against the LORD."**

Ellicott notes a wordplay: "I will cast thee" is literally "I send thee" — the same verb used in v. 15 for "the LORD has not sent thee." God says with emphatic irony: "You were not sent by me, but I will send you — off the face of the earth." (https://mail.biblehub.com/commentaries/ellicott/jeremiah/28.htm)

JFB highlights the time correspondence: "The prediction was uttered in the fifth month (v. 1); Hananiah's death took place in the seventh month — i.e., within two months after the prediction — answering with awful significance to the two years in which Hananiah had foretold that the yoke imposed by Babylon would end." (https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/jfu/jeremiah-28.html)

Gill says the death would not be natural but "violent death, by the immediate hand of God, by some judgment upon him." (https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/geb/jeremiah-28.html)

The charge "you have preached rebellion against the LORD" is significant. Hananiah's message, which sounded patriotic and hopeful, was actually rebellion — because it contradicted God's revealed will that Judah submit to Babylon. JFB: "opposition to God's plain direction that all should submit to Babylon." (https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/jfu/jeremiah-28.html)

---

### v. 17

**"And in the seventh month of that very year, the prophet Hananiah died."**

Hananiah prophesied in the fifth month; he died in the seventh month — just two months later. JFB notes that this swift fulfillment "answered with awful significance to the two years in which Hananiah had foretold that the yoke imposed by Babylon would end." (https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/jfu/jeremiah-28.html)

David Guzik: "Two months is not a long time, but it is plenty of time to repent if one has any inclination to repent." (https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/jeremiah-28/)

Adam Clarke (cited in Enduring Word): "God, in mercy, gave him about two months, in which he might prepare to meet his Judge. Here, then the true prophet was demonstrated, and the false prophet detected. The death of Hananiah, thus predicted, was God's seal to the words of his prophet; and must have gained his other predictions great credit among the people." (https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/jeremiah-28/)

Gill mentions a Jewish tradition recorded in the Targum: Hananiah, knowing Jeremiah's prophecy, instructed his family to hide his death until after the new year began (in the seventh month, Tishri), hoping to make Jeremiah appear a liar. But the text says plainly he died in the seventh month. (https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/geb/jeremiah-28.html)

Precept Austin adds a sobering reflection: "Yet, despite such a striking confirmation, the response of the nation reveals the stubbornness of the human heart, for even this dramatic demonstration of divine truth did not lead them to forsake their sins or return in genuine repentance to the God of Israel." (https://www.preceptaustin.org/jeremiah-28-commentary)

---

## Where Protestant Traditions Differ

The differences among Protestant traditions on Jeremiah 28 are not sharply defined — most traditions read the chapter similarly as a confrontation between true and false prophecy. However, some distinct emphases emerge:

**Reformed / Presbyterian:** The JFB commentary emphasizes divine sovereignty — God as "the great First Cause" behind even the iron yoke (v. 14). The JFB application stresses that false teachers who set aside the Lord's yoke "bring upon their hearers and upon themselves an infinitely more galling yoke" — drawing a contrast between the "easy yoke" of Christ and the "yoke of bondage" of the law (Acts 15:10; Galatians 5:1). (https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/jfu/jeremiah-28.html)

**Baptist:** Both Gill (Particular Baptist) and Garner-Howes (Baptist) treat the chapter in a straightforward historical-grammatical manner. Gill focuses on careful textual details (the dating, the Hebrew wording). Spurgeon, quoted in the Preacher's Homiletical Commentary and Enduring Word, makes applications about the yoke of sin versus the yoke of Christ: "A man shall carry a bucket of water on his head and be very tired of the burden; but the same man when he dives into the sea shall have thousands of buckets on his head without perceiving their weight, because he is in the element and it entirely surrounds him." (https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/phc/jeremiah-28.html)

**Pentecostal / Charismatic (Enduring Word):** David Guzik's commentary emphasizes the personal and devotional application heavily — the danger of "smooth" messages that please the ear, the need to test teaching against Scripture, and the principle that rejecting God's gentle correction brings harsher discipline. Guzik also highlights the emotional dimension (Jeremiah's "Amen" as partly ironic, the pain of being publicly contradicted). His application repeatedly ties the wooden/iron yoke imagery to Matthew 11:28–30. (https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/jeremiah-28/)

---

## Other Views and Traditions

**Jewish tradition (cited in Gill and JFB):** The Targum and some rabbinic sources hold that Hananiah died on the eve of the new year (the last day of the sixth month) and ordered his family to conceal his death until the seventh month had begun, hoping to make Jeremiah appear a false prophet. Gill dismisses this as making "the difficulty greater, and contradicts the very text, which says, he died in the seventh month." (https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/geb/jeremiah-28.html)

**Catholic and Orthodox readings, modern scholarship, and Wesleyan/Methodist/Lutheran specific commentaries:** Searches within the allowed sites did not return accessible results for these traditions' distinct readings of Jeremiah 28. The Catholic Haydock Commentary is listed among StudyLight.org's resources but its content was not reachable within the fetch limits. Similarly, modern scholarly sources (bibleodyssey.org, netbible.org) were not reached. The NET Bible notes are quoted briefly in Precept Austin (on the meaning of "yoke") but no full NET commentary on the chapter was retrieved.

---

## Summary of Key Themes Across All Sources

1. **The test of a true prophet:** Fulfillment (Deuteronomy 18:22) and consistency with prior revelation (Isaiah 8:20).
2. **The danger of pleasant lies:** Hananiah's message was patriotic, hopeful, and popular — and utterly false.
3. **Rejecting God's gentle discipline brings harsher discipline:** Wooden yokes become iron yokes.
4. **God's sovereignty over nations:** Even Nebuchadnezzar is God's servant.
5. **The patience and restraint of the true prophet:** Jeremiah said "Amen," then walked away, then waited for God's word.
6. **God vindicates His true messengers:** Hananiah's death within two months confirmed Jeremiah's authenticity.
